subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The McLaren F1
description: A quick, practical guide to The McLaren F1.

hook.text: Gordon Murray wanted to build the ultimate road car. He put the driver in the center—like a fighter jet.

buildup.text: The 1992 McLaren F1 had a BMW V12, gold-foil engine bay insulation, and no electronic aids at all.

discovery.text: It hit 240 mph—the fastest production car in the world for over a decade.

twist.text: Only 106 were built. McLaren chose exclusivity over profit and never mass-produced it.

climax.text: Today, McLaren F1s sell for over $20 million. It's the most valuable modern car in existence.

punchline.text: The ultimate car was built without compromise—literally.

quiz.question: Where did the McLaren F1 place the driver?

details.summary: The McLaren F1, engineered by Gordon Murray in 1992, used a gold-lined engine bay, carbon fiber monocoque, and central driving position to create arguably the greatest supercar ever built.
details.whyItMatters: The F1 set the top speed record at 240 mph in 1998 and held it for years. Its engineering purity and no-compromise philosophy created a car that appreciates in value like fine art.
takeaways: Its BMW V12 engine was the most powerful naturally aspirated road-car engine
The central driving position placed the driver at the car's axis
Only 106 were built, with prices now exceeding 20 million dollars

faq.question: Why is the McLaren F1 so expensive today?
faq.answer: Only 106 were made, and each is a masterpiece of engineering. Combined with its speed record legacy, racing pedigree at Le Mans, and growing collector demand, prices have risen to over 20 million dollars.

faq.question: Why was gold used in the engine bay?
faq.answer: Gold is an excellent heat reflector. Gordon Murray lined the engine bay with gold foil to protect surrounding carbon fiber from the V12's extreme heat, choosing engineering effectiveness over cost concerns.
